children.title: Cell Division & Homeostasis
children.description: The cell cycle, how mitosis and meiosis differ in purpose and outcome, and how the body holds its internal conditions steady through negative feedback.

children.title: The Cell Cycle
children.description: Grow and copy DNA, then divide — and why the order can't be broken.

teach.headline: Grow, Copy DNA, Then Divide
teach.body:
The cell cycle has two big parts. During **interphase** the cell grows and copies all of its DNA (the S phase). Then **mitosis** divides the nucleus into two identical sets of chromosomes, and **cytokinesis** splits the cytoplasm into two cells.

Order matters: the DNA must be copied and the chromosomes separated **before** the cell splits. If cytokinesis happens too early, each new cell gets the wrong amount of DNA and organelles — and likely dies.

![Circular diagram of cell cycle phases from interphase through mitosis](/content/bio-eoc/figures/bio_eoc_cell_cycle.svg)

figures.alt: Cell cycle circle showing interphase, prophase, metaphase, anaphase, and telophase phases
figures.caption: DNA replicates during interphase before mitosis begins.

teach.mnemonic: COPY BEFORE YOU CUT. Interphase copies DNA → mitosis sorts it → cytokinesis splits the cell.
teach.poweredIdea: Interphase copies the DNA; mitosis then cytokinesis split it into two identical cells — order matters.

data.prompt: A cell copies all of its DNA before dividing during the stage called _____.
data.hint: The long 'growing and copying' stage before mitosis

data.prompt: On the cell cycle diagram, the stage where DNA is copied before division is _____.
data.hint: The largest segment before mitosis begins

data.processTitle: The cell cycle — arrange the stages in order
data.mnemonic: I-PMAT-C: Interphase, then Prophase, Metaphase, Anaphase, Telophase, Cytokinesis.

steps.title: Interphase — grow and copy DNA
steps.consequenceHint: DNA must be copied before the cell can divide.

steps.title: Prophase — chromosomes condense
steps.consequenceHint: Chromosomes condense so they can be moved.

steps.title: Metaphase — chromosomes line up at the middle
steps.consequenceHint: They must align before they can be split evenly.

steps.title: Anaphase — sister chromatids separate
steps.consequenceHint: Identical copies are pulled to opposite poles.

steps.title: Telophase — two nuclei reform
steps.consequenceHint: A nucleus rebuilds around each chromosome set.

steps.title: Cytokinesis — the cytoplasm splits in two
steps.consequenceHint: The cell only splits after the nucleus has divided.

causalLinks.why: Chromosomes can only condense after the DNA has been copied.
Chromatids separate only after they line up at the middle.
The cell divides only after two nuclei have formed.

data.story: An error causes a cell to go through cytokinesis (splitting in two) before it completes mitosis (separating its chromosomes).
data.question: Which best describes the new cells?
data.answer: They have an incorrect amount of DNA and organelles and will likely experience cell death.
options: They have an incorrect amount of DNA and organelles and will likely experience cell death.
They are each double the size of the original cell.
They each have exactly twice the normal amount of DNA.
They have no DNA but keep cycling through the cell cycle.
data.explanation: Splitting before the chromosomes are separated gives each daughter cell the wrong amount of DNA and organelles, so the cells usually die.

data.correct: The cell grows and copies its DNA
distractors: Sister chromatids separate to the poles
The cytoplasm splits into two cells
Chromosomes line up at the cell's middle

achievement.flavor: You order the cell cycle and see why splitting before sorting the chromosomes dooms the cell.

children.title: Mitosis vs Meiosis
children.description: Two divisions with different jobs: identical body cells versus varied gametes.

teach.headline: Two Identical vs Four Varied Cells
teach.body:
**Mitosis** makes **two genetically identical, diploid (2n)** body cells — the division used for growth and repair.

**Meiosis** makes **four genetically varied, haploid (n)** sex cells, or **gametes** — the division used for sexual reproduction. Diploid means two sets of chromosomes; haploid means one. Only meiosis halves the chromosome number; mitosis keeps it the same.
teach.mnemonic: MEIO = LESSEN. MEIOSIS halves the chromosomes → 4 varied gametes. MITOSIS = 2 identical copies.
teach.poweredIdea: Mitosis makes 2 identical diploid body cells; meiosis makes 4 varied haploid gametes.

data.prompt: A cell that has two complete sets of chromosomes is described as _____.
data.hint: Two sets; the opposite of haploid

data.paragraph: Skin cells use mitosis to repair a cut, and the body also uses mitosis to produce the sperm and egg cells needed for reproduction.
data.bugPhrase: uses mitosis to produce the sperm and egg cells needed for reproduction
data.hint: Which division halves the chromosome number to make sex cells?
data.canonicalFix: Gametes (sperm and egg) are produced by meiosis, which halves the chromosome number. Mitosis makes identical diploid body cells for growth and repair.
data.poweredIdea: Mitosis makes body cells; meiosis makes the gametes used in reproduction.

distractors: Makes two identical diploid body cells

data.story: A dividing cell produces four cells, each with half the original chromosome number and each genetically different from the others.
data.question: Which process produced these cells?
data.explanation: Four genetically varied cells with half the chromosome number are the signature of meiosis.

achievement.flavor: You split the two divisions by their output: identical diploid copies versus varied haploid gametes.

children.title: Maintaining Homeostasis
children.description: Holding internal conditions steady while the outside world changes.

teach.headline: Keeping the Inside Steady
teach.body:
**Homeostasis** is keeping internal conditions stable even as the outside world changes — temperature, water balance, pH, and blood sugar all stay near a target **set point**.

Cells and organ systems constantly sense changes and respond to stay balanced. The selectively permeable cell membrane is one tool: it lets needed materials in and waste out to hold conditions steady.
teach.mnemonic: HOMEO = SAME. STASIS = STANDING. Homeostasis = STAY THE SAME inside while outside shifts.
teach.poweredIdea: Homeostasis is maintaining stable internal conditions near a set point despite outside change.

data.prompt: Maintaining stable internal conditions despite changes outside the body is called _____.

data.story: On a hot day a person sweats to cool off; on a cold day the same person shivers to warm up.
data.question: What is the body maintaining through these responses?
data.answer: Homeostasis — a stable internal body temperature
options: Homeostasis — a stable internal body temperature
A change in the body's DNA
data.explanation: Sweating and shivering both work to keep internal temperature near its set point — that is homeostasis.

data.mnemonic: HOMEO = SAME. STASIS = STANDING. Homeostasis means staying the SAME on the inside.

achievement.flavor: You read sweating and shivering as the body holding its internal conditions near a set point.

children.title: Negative Feedback Loops
children.description: Loops that reverse a change to steer the body back to its set point.

teach.headline: A Loop That Reverses the Change
teach.body:
A **negative feedback** loop detects a change and triggers a response that pushes the condition **back toward the set point** — it reverses the change.

Blood glucose: after a meal it rises, the pancreas releases insulin, cells take up glucose, and the level falls back to normal. Body temperature: too hot triggers sweating, too cold triggers shivering. The response always counteracts the original change.
teach.mnemonic: NEGATIVE = REVERSE. Too high → push DOWN. Too low → push UP. Always steer back to the set point.
teach.poweredIdea: Negative feedback detects a change and triggers a response that reverses it back to the set point.

data.scenario: After eating a large meal, the glucose level in a person's blood rises above normal.
data.predictPrompt: How does the body bring blood glucose back to normal?
predictOptions: The pancreas releases more glucose, so the level rises further
The pancreas releases insulin; cells absorb glucose and the level falls back to normal
Nothing happens until the next meal
The body permanently resets its normal glucose level higher
data.runNarrative: Sensors detect the high glucose. The pancreas releases insulin, which signals body cells to take up glucose from the blood. As cells absorb it, blood glucose falls back toward the set point.
data.truthSummary: Negative feedback reverses the change: a rise in glucose triggers a response that lowers it back to normal.

bugCandidates.label: I thought the body adds more glucose to match the meal
bugCandidates.explanation: That would amplify the change — positive feedback. Homeostasis uses negative feedback, which reverses the change.

bugCandidates.label: I forgot that a sensor must detect the change first
bugCandidates.explanation: True, but the headline error is amplifying instead of reversing the change.

bugCandidates.label: I assumed the set point itself shifts higher
bugCandidates.explanation: The set point stays the same; the body steers the value back toward it.

data.poweredIdea: Negative feedback lowers high blood glucose back to its set point — it reverses, not amplifies.

data.prompt: A feedback loop that reverses a change to return to the set point is called _____ feedback.
data.hint: It counteracts the change rather than amplifying it

data.correct: A response that reverses the change
distractors: A response that amplifies the change
A one-time event with no sensor
A permanent change to the set point

data.story: A person's body temperature rises during exercise, so they begin to sweat, which cools the body back down.
data.question: What type of control does this describe?
data.explanation: The cooling response counteracts the rise in temperature, returning the body toward its set point — negative feedback.

achievement.flavor: You trace a loop that senses a change and pushes the body back toward its set point.
